[/page/8/Text/11]
IPA is well suited for studying a small sample of four participants (drawn from a larger sample of a bigger study) who experienced a particular phenomenon (attempted suicide) (Smith and Osman 2003).

The study used qualitative data, which was collected as part of the research component of a Master's degree in Psychology (Meissner 2013). ... The analysis of the larger data set has been published elsewhere (Meissner, Bantjes, and Kagee 2016).

[/page/1/Text/7] Participants' accounts of suicidal behaviour revealed a struggle for relatedness and autonomy. Two major themes were identified: (1) 'Turning away from others and self', which describes how participants disconnect from close others and from self, prior to attempting suicide as an act of autonomy; and (2) 'Returning to self and others', which describes the process of healing and recovery from being suicidal through re-connecting with others and gaining a healthy sense of autonomy.

Two key themes emerged from the interview data. The first theme 'Turning away from others and self', described participants' experience of disconnection from self and others and their wish for autonomy prior to and at the time of attempting suicide. The second theme 'Returning to the self and others', captured participants' experience of feeling re-connected with their self and with others, and gaining a healthy sense of autonomy following their suicide attempt.

All participants indicated that their relationships with their parents prior to attempting suicide was distant owing to arguments and fights, the emotional unavailability of their parents as well as strict and controlling parenting strategies. All participants stated that they felt particularly disconnected from their fathers, and expressed sadness, anger and resentment at their fathers' lack of emotional involvement in their lives. Mark and Andrew said that their parents' lack of attention and affection made them feel alone and as a result of this, they wished to become 'independent' from their parents. All participants also indicated that they were subject to the rules and expectations of their parents, which made them feel 'trapped' or 'controlled'. Brian explained: 'My father would overpower the family; his rules or no rules. So that's why I felt that, you know, I couldn't breathe.' and Johan said: 'My dad was a corporal and he is extremely strict. He had a firm hand when he raised me. So speaking to him about failure, that you did something wrong, is impossible.' All participants said that they imagined that if they were dead they would be able to escape feeling trapped and they could then express their separateness and independence from their parents.

evidence.section_title: Another chance at living and loving
evidence.quote: All participants viewed their survival as a re-birth or new beginning. They said that following their suicide attempt, they were able to identify a reason for living. Their suicidal crisis appeared to provide them with an opportunity to reconnect with people close to them and find existential meaning in relationships. For example, Andrew said: One of the things that actually drew me away from that [suicidal behaviour] was just the bible verse of without love we are nothing … The only reason to live is to be there for others. All participants reflected that after their suicide attempt they no longer 'rebelled' against their religion. Two participants broke away from their religion and two participants developed a view of God as caring, rather than punitive. Mark said: 'I believe God is a gentleman. You can do suicide if you want to, but he gives you the alternatives and the ways out.' Engaging in meditation and prayer assisted the participants to rekindle their relationship with God. All participants also remarked that they shifted from being preoccupied with themselves to being aware of others close to them, and the impact the suicide attempt had on these others.
